items.title: The more you know, the harder it is to change someone’s mind
items.summary: Here’s the bad news: The deeper your understanding of an issue and the stronger your conviction about the solution, the worse you often become at persuasion. This isn’t a character flaw; it’s a law of neuroscience. Once you understand it, you’ll stop wondering why your brilliant ideas and proposals keep floundering in meeting rooms. It’s due to a cognitive trap that the fields of behavioral economics and neuroscience have spent decades documenting: the curse of knowledge . Once I explain how it works, you’ll start to recognize why it’s working against your persuasion. In the early 1990s, Stanford graduate student Elizabeth Newton designed a simple experiment that revealed something profound about human cognition. She divided participants into two groups: “tappers” and “listeners.” Tappers were given a list of well-known songs like “Happy Birthday to You” and “The Star-Spangled Banner” — simple tunes everyone knows. They were asked to tap out a song’s rhythm on a table while a listener tried to identify it. Before they began, tappers were asked to predict how often listeners would correctly identify the song. The tappers predicted a 50% success rate — after all, these were famous songs, and the rhythms were distinctive. They felt confident they could tap them out clearly. The actual success rate? Out of 120 songs tapped, listeners correctly identified only 3 — a success rate of 2.5%. This result shocked the tappers. The rhythm was clear and unmistakable to them as they tapped. How could the listeners not hear the song perfectly? What the tappers didn’t realize was that they had a fundamentally different experience from their listeners. When you tap out “Happy Birthday to You,” you hear the melody in your head. The song is complete and vivid in your mind. The listeners, however, hear something completely different: disconnected taps, with no underlying melody. They’re trying to identify a song from percussion alone, which is nearly impossible even for familiar tunes. Here’s the frustrating part: The tapper cannot experience what the listener is experiencing in the moment. Once you hear the melody, you cannot tap the rhythm without that melody playing in your head, but the listener hears only the taps. In other words, your knowledge has fundamentally altered your perception of what you believe others are experiencing. This is the curse of knowledge. And it doesn’t just apply to tapping songs. It applies to your persuasion, especially when you are the well-informed expert in the room. As you are about to learn from three economists, experts are lousy at thinking like their audiences. Why experts fail to persuade Economists Colin Camerer, George Loewenstein, and Martin Weber published a paper that challenged beliefs about how informed people predict the judgment of less-informed people. Economic models assumed that experts could accurately anticipate how novices would think. The researchers discovered something very surprising, however: Experts were systematically biased predictors. Building on psychologist Baruch Fischhoff’s earlier work on hindsight bias — the tendency to believe, once you know an outcome, that you would have predicted it all along — they found that once someone acquired knowledge or expertise, they became anchored in that more-informed state of mind. When asked to predict what someone without that knowledge would think or do, experts could not mentally set aside what they knew. They were pulled inevitably toward their informed perspective rather than the other person’s. This curse of knowledge functions like a cognitive undertow. It becomes extraordinarily difficult to escape back to the state of not knowing, even temporarily and even when it would serve you to do so — especially when it comes to persuasion. Here’s how this curse blindsides you in persuasion. You’ve spent weeks developing a proposal to solve a complex problem. You’ve acquired deep knowledge about the problem as well as considered several solutions and their trade-offs. You’ve thought through objections and counterarguments. You’ve found evidence that makes one solution stand out above the others. You’re now completely convinced of the way forward. By the time you present your proposal to decision-makers, you’re already deep in the curse of knowledge. You cannot accurately imagine what your proposal sounds like to anyone who’s encountering it for the first time. You cannot appreciate their state of ignorance or alternate perspective because you’re anchored in your state of knowledge. While you need to simplify, translate, and educate your decision-makers, you instead persuade from the perspective of complexity and conviction. The various cognitive traps associated with the curse of knowledge distance you from your stakeholders’ perspectives, pushing you away from genuine engagement and ultimately leading you to persuasive impotence. Now you can start to understand the baffling experience all of us have had: presenting what feels like an obvious and clear case for an idea and watching it hit a brick wall. From our perspective, everything is clear, logical, and persuasive. From our stakeholders’ perspective, we’re tapping out a rhythm to a song they can’t hear. What is playing in our heads — all that analysis, all those supporting arguments and evidence — is inaudible to them. To further complicate matters, we become invested in a solution — “our” solution. Pride of ownership deepens our commitment. When stakeholders start to raise challenging questions, we say to ourselves: They must not be listening carefully. They must be resistant to change or protective of the status quo. The possibility that we’ve failed to build a bridge from their knowledge to ours doesn’t even occur to us, because we cannot see the gap. The antidote to the curse of knowledge There is an antidote to overcoming these psychological traps, but it requires a dramatic reframing of your understanding of the act of persuasion. You must abandon your mental model of persuasion as first and foremost a solution-centric activity*. Yes, at some point, you will start championing a particular solution, but only after an intensive exploration into the problem as well as its impact on key stakeholders. The core lesson here is that masterful persuasion starts with problem definition — not solution definition. It’s not an easy perspective to accept. After all, you want to solve a problem efficiently and quickly. And who can resist the ego rewards of “pride of ownership” and the public recognition of how clever you are? Instead, with problem-centric persuasion, you’ll experience a different kind of reward: meaningful collaborations with colleagues in solving truly thorny problems. items.title: My Imaginary Dad Has a Very Real Oscar
items.summary: Joon-Ho My father is always away, directing movies to great acclaim. A man throws himself into the jaws of the sea monster that’s kidnapped his daughter. A woman bludgeons a stranger to death and sets his house ablaze to protect her son from imprisonment. You see, says my father through his movies, I understand what it means to love you so much. A cinematic god, people say, is my father. His latest film garnered worldwide praise. “I’m ready to drink tonight,” he tells reporters at the Oscars after-party. He holds up two of his trophies and clinks their faces to make them kiss. I lift my glass. Cheers, I say to my television. This toast is in your honor. Though I don’t possess my father’s drinking abilities, I push through discomfort when there’s cause for celebration. We’re alike in other ways. For instance, my father is an anti-capitalist. I’ve watched his movies wherein he foregrounds the worker’s struggle. I locate his ethic in the daeri driver, in the kind-hearted girl who befriends the giant, slaughter-bred pig, in the weary face of the basement dweller whose home floods with municipal wastewater. I know he’s teaching me, specifically, by way of cinema. I tell my friends, He’s a director of and for the people. You’ve never even met him, my friends remind me. Soon, I say. Soon, we will meet, and he will recognize exactly who I am. His beautiful translator follows him onto the Golden Globes press stage. He gazes at her, and she gazes at him, and they smile at each other. The Hollywood Reporter takes their picture. “She’s perfect,” says my father of his translator. “We all depend on her.” Of course, I feel his swell of pride in my bones. There she is, beside him on his media tours, ushering forth elegant interpretations of my father’s thoughts such that I might hear his voice as she’s come to know it. I’m indebted to you, Sharon, I say to my television. You’re helping him in a way I never could. You’re helping me in a way he never could. “This is so embarrassing,” she says to The Hollywood Reporter . The press crowd laughs, and I laugh too. When I switch off my television, I return to my mind’s dull present. I feel the sickening threat of a deadline commingling with my want to be somewhere else. Like hunger, my debts grow larger because I continue to live. Thus, at some point I will have to make several crucial decisions, will accept the need to sell my few possessions. I will pawn my television in order to stay in the place I call home. In the end, we all must do what’s best when circumstances demand some type of sacrifice. And the situation is only temporary. I will one day repossess this important medium. Perhaps a nicer screen mounted to a nicer wall I’ve painted yellow. Perhaps by then I’ll have built a family of my own. A family for whom I’d do anything. I can see my life like it’s unfolding right before me. My friends will gather at my warm apartment for a viewing party, complete with cocktails. So bourgeois, I’ll say, clinking my glass to another glass. Turn on the subtitles, my friends will insist. Shh, I’ll say. The kids are asleep. The film will delight and move us, will render the world, such as it is, through a dystopian, cautionary fable shot through by moments of stunning humanity. When the time finally comes, I will whisper, Hello. The credits will roll, and my friends will rise from the couch. It’s me, I’ll whisper, my face reflected on the screen. items.title: A fake Einstein quote actually explains the affordability crisis
items.summary: One of the most famous quotes commonly attributed to Einstein was something that he himself never actually said: “Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn’t, pays it.” While the quote is not from Einstein at all, the math behind the concept of compound interest is incredibly profound, playing a role in any system — physical, mathematical, or financial — that accumulates based on how much of a base amount is present. When the base amount increases, it isn’t just the original amount (the principal) that continues to accumulate, but the additional amount (the interest) that adds to the accumulation as well. While investors most often use this to explain the growth of wealth in an interest-bearing account, it can be applied not just to wealth, but to the cost and price of goods and commodities that continue to increase over time as well. When wealth increases, we call it compound interest, but when prices increase, we call it inflation: not the cosmic kind , but the economic kind . The Einstein quote may be a fake, or at least grossly misattributed, but if you want to understand the current affordability crisis, the mathematics and the concept behind the quote is exactly what everyone should understand. Here’s how it works. This image shows Albert Einstein playing his violin in 1932. While Einstein had a great many famous quotes and sayings over his life, there is no evidence he ever remarked anything about compound interest, or called it “the greatest invention” or the “eighth wonder of the world” or anything of that ilk. It appears that was an invention of a New York Times writer from 1983. Credit: Bettmann Collection / Getty Images The story behind the quote Einstein grew to fame in the early 20th century, and died in 1955. While an enormous amount of his writings, speeches, and interviews survive, nothing that he ever said or wrote relating to compound interest survives. The earliest assertion that the quote was said by Einstein can be traced back to a 1983 New York Times column , which mentions the quote as a popular saying that’s attributed to him. But it’s likely that the attribution was made up entirely, as there is no print record of the quote — or any saying linking Einstein to the concept of compound interest — prior to that. An investigation into the quote’s origins unearthed two very similar statements that may provide the ultimate inspiration for the eventual saying that became linked with Einstein’s name. In 1916, a newspaper advertisement in California described compound interest as “the greatest invention the world has ever produced.” A little bit later, in 1925, the phrase “the eighth wonder of the world is compound interest” was used by a Cleveland savings and loan company. It is unknown what sort of intersection of: fabrication, marketing by financial firms looking for investment, and antisemitic thoughts (about the link between Einstein, Jews, and banks), played a role in conferring an Einsteinian attribution to the actual quote itself. This height by age chart, published in 2000 by the CDC, shows a roughly linear growth in height in boys from the age of 2 until adulthood. There is no compounding in humans when it comes to increases in height; the increase comes instead in a linear fashion. Credit : CDC The math of compound interest When most of us think of growth, we think of what’s known as linear growth: where things grow by a given amount over a given interval. If you have a child and the child grows by 7.6 centimeters (3 inches) per year, then a baby who’s initially born at 51 centimeters (20 inches) will, after 17 years, have grown to a height of 180 centimeters (5 feet 11 inches). In linear growth, the amount that you gain does not depend on the amount that you already have. Instead, the growth is by a fixed amount over a given time. Financially, it would be like getting $100 every year on your birthday: after 17 years, you would have $1700. On the other hand, compound interest accumulates based on the base amount that you already have. If you accumulate interest at a 4% rate annually, then if you start with $100, how much will you have after 17 years? You might think — and this is incorrect, linear thinking — that you should just multiply that 4% by 17 years, giving you 68%, growing your $100 to $168. But the way compound interest works is different. For the first year, you earn 4% interest on $100, giving you $104. For the second year, you earn 4% interest on $104, giving you $108.16. For the third year, you earn 4% interest on $108.16, giving you $112.49. For the fourth year, you earn 4% interest on $112.49, giving you $116.99. And so on. Note that for each year beyond the first, you don’t just gain $4 a year (the 4% of the initial $100), but more than $4, as you get 4% interest on the full amount of your balance. By the time a full 17 years have elapsed, your initial $100 will have grown to $194.79: a significant increase over the $168 you’d expect with linear growth. The idea of compound interest is that instead of just gaining the same amount year-after-year on your initial investment, the interest that you earn gets re-invested alongside the principal, where they both earn interest together. Over long periods of time, this can add up to a tremendous advantage over “linear” interest and growth alone. Credit : Pixy/CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 There are three factors that matter when it comes to compound interest. The first is simple: the rate of growth, known as the interest rate. If we took that same analysis — starting with $100 and growing it for 17 years — but upped the interest rate to 5%, 7%, or 9%, that initial investment would instead have grown to $229.20, $315.88, or $432.76, respectively after those 17 years elapsed. The second is also simple: the duration of time of the investment. If we go back to that original 4% interest rate, but consider longer-term investments, we can see how continued growth helps increase the amount that you gain. If you wait 30 years, 50 years, or (generationally) 250 years, your initial $100 would grow to $324.34, $710.67, or $1,812,737.11, respectively, at that same 4% rate. Time makes an enormous difference when it comes to compound interest, especially over the long run. The third is a little more complicated: how often the interest is compounded. In the prior examples, we compounded the interest annually: we calculated the interest based on how much we had as the principal amount at the start of the year, and then added the interest to the balance at the end of the year, where it becomes part of the new principal. After 17 years, if we compounded the interest quarterly, monthly, or daily, then instead of $194.79, we’d have $196.72, $197.16, or $197.38. All three of these factors matter for the same underlying reason: interest gives you growth, and the amount of growth you get is determined by both the interest rate and the principal amount. When you grow the principal, you get interest not just on the original balance, but on the “amount of growth” too, and this accumulates over time. This graph shows the difference of a 20 year investment that accrues 10% in simple interest per year (gaining 10% of the original principal value, annually) versus 10% compounding interest, where after each year, the interest is added back into the principal and begins accruing interest as well. The greater the amount of time that passes, the more the two curves depart from one another.
